KEY MESSAGE 1...There continues to be an elevated risk for severe 
thunderstorms and flash flooding today and Wednesday, with the 
greater risk this afternoon and this evening.

A strong upper-level trough is forecast to pivot into and across the 
Northeast and Mid-Atlantic later this afternoon and tonight, then 
remain in place through Wednesday. This will drive surface low 
pressure well to our north, however an associated warm front will 
lift north across our region today followed by a cold front late 
this afternoon and tonight.

An increase in the low-level warm air advection this morning 
will be enhanced by a southerly low-level jet of about 30 knots.
This is providing lift within a moistening air mass to generate
some showers and thunderstorms this morning, with this mainly 
focused north and west of I-95. There is some 850 mb convergence
north of I-78 early this morning, and this is within an axis of
increasing instability. This is likely driving the ongoing 
cluster of convection moving northeastward across our far 
northwest zones. These cells should be faster moving therefore 
the flash flood risk should remain limited. As a warm front 
advances northward, increasing dew points and at least some 
sunshine should promote plenty of instability this afternoon and
evening. The northward movement of the warm front will 
determine the extent of the greater instability. The low-level 
flow is more backed through the morning before it starts to veer
some this afternoon, therefore will need to watch for some 
rotation if stronger convective elements (more discrete) can 
become realized by early afternoon. As the main upper-level 
trough arrives during the afternoon and the surface cold front 
also starts to approach, strong mid to upper level flow will 
foster greater forcing for ascent. This is expected to result in
an increase in convective development, especially to our west, 
with an initial focus along a pre- frontal trough. Convection 
should tend to organize into clusters or one or more line 
segments as the low- level flow veers some more by evening. This
veering however will be delayed though if the warm front is 
slower to advance northward, therefore any stronger cells that 
especially interact with the warm front will need to be watched 
more closely for a tornado risk. Otherwise, tall initial CAPE 
profiles may tend to widen some into this evening and with steep
low-level lapse rates the DCAPE will increase. Areas of 
damaging straight-line winds will be the main severe weather 
hazard, with this potentially becoming more enhanced if 
convection develops a cold pool with bowing segments. Some more 
robust convective cores could produce severe hail. The severe 
risk will continue for a time this evening as instability may 
remain favorable as the upper-level trough amplifies some into 
the region. Convection may tend to become messy with competing 
outflows which could also enhance the locally heavy rain/flash 
flooding risk.

Another risk is areas of excessive rainfall that could lead to flash 
flooding. As a warm front lifts northward, winds turn more southerly 
with moisture being transported northward. Precipitable water values 
are forecast to surge to 2.00-2.25 inches in the wake of the warm 
front. Within the warm air advection burst through this morning, 
some convection is anticipated especially north and west of I-95. 
While this activity could produce locally heavy rain, storm motions 
should limit this. The warm front may stall near the NJ/NY/PA 
border, but this is uncertain. As additional convection develops 
this afternoon and evening, deeper convection will likely increase 
the rainfall rates with the strong convective cores capable of 
producing 1-3 inches per hour. Some areas are saturated, especially 
in northern NJ and portions of the Philadelphia metro, which remain 
more vulnerable to excessive rainfall after this past several days. 
Excessive rainfall rates, especially for the urban areas, could lead 
to flash flooding. This risk will become enhanced where convection 
ends up being more focused. There will be some areas that could get 
2-4 inches of rain while some areas get much less. Given the 
continued risk for flash flooding across the urban corridor, a Flash 
Flood Watch remains in effect for today through later tonight 
(the main time frame looks to be this afternoon and this evening).

On Wednesday, the cold front will sag farther south and east and 
depending on how quickly this clears our area there will be some 
showers and thunderstorms, especially as additional shortwaves move 
through the flow within the upper-level trough overhead. This looks 
to be more concentrated across southern New Jersey to Delmarva but 
could extend into the I-95 corridor for a time. There is some severe 
weather risk mainly near and south/east of the I-95 corridor with 
locally damaging wind gusts the main threat. The greater instability 
and shear looks to reside across Delma
